paragraphs: A fifth class of provisions favoring the federal authority consists of the following restrictions on the individual States:

1. "No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts; or grant any title of nobility."

The ban on treaties, alliances, and confederations is already part of the existing Articles of the Union, and for reasons that need no explanation it is copied into the new Constitution. The ban on letters of marque also comes from the old system, but the new Constitution extends it somewhat. Under the old Articles, the States could grant letters of marque once war had been declared. Under the new Constitution, these licenses must come from the government of the United States, in wartime and before any declaration of war alike. The change is fully justified by the advantage of uniformity in everything that concerns foreign powers, and by the advantage of immediate responsibility to the nation for every act that the nation itself will be answerable for.

The Confederation left the right of coining money in the hands of the States, which this clause now takes from them. They held it alongside Congress, subject to one exception: Congress alone had the right to regulate the alloy and value. Here, too, the new provision improves on the old. So long as the general authority fixed the alloy and value, a right of coinage in the particular States could do nothing except multiply expensive mints and vary the forms and weights of the coins in circulation. That second problem defeats one of the purposes for which the power was first given to the federal head. The first might spare the inconvenience of shipping gold and silver to a central mint for recoinage, but local mints established under the general authority can serve that end just as well.

Every citizen must be pleased that the prohibition now reaches bills of credit, in proportion to his love of justice and his knowledge of the true sources of public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered from the pestilent effects of paper money on the confidence needed between man and man, on the confidence needed in the public councils, on the industry and morals of the people, and on the character of republican government. These losses are an enormous debt, chargeable against the States that adopted this unwise measure, and it must long remain unpaid. Or rather, they are an accumulated guilt that can be expiated only by one thing: a voluntary sacrifice, on the altar of justice, of the very power that has been the instrument of it. Beyond these persuasive considerations, we may observe that the same reasons that show the necessity of denying the States the power of regulating coin prove equally that they should not be free to put a paper medium in the place of coin. If every State had a right to regulate the value of its coin, there might be as many currencies as there are States, and dealings among them would be obstructed. Its value could be altered retroactively, which would injure the citizens of other States and kindle animosities among the States themselves. Subjects of foreign powers might suffer in the same way, and so the Union would be discredited and drawn into quarrels by the indiscretion of a single member. A power in the States to emit paper money is no less open to every one of these harms than a power to coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts is withdrawn from the States on the same principle as the power to issue a paper currency.

Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing the obligation of contracts violate the first principles of the social compact and every principle of sound legislation. The declarations prefixed to some of the State constitutions expressly forbid the first two, and the spirit and scope of these fundamental charters forbid all three. Our own experience has taught us, nevertheless, that we should not neglect to add further fences against these dangers. The Convention was entirely right, then, to add this constitutional bulwark for personal security and private rights. And I am much mistaken if, in doing so, they have not served the genuine feelings of their constituents as faithfully as their undoubted interests. The sober people of America are weary of the shifting policy that has guided the public councils. They have seen with regret and indignation that sudden changes and legislative interference in matters affecting personal rights become profitable schemes in the hands of enterprising and influential speculators, and snares for the more industrious and less informed part of the community. They have seen, too, that one legislative interference is only the first link in a long chain of repetitions, each later interference being naturally produced by the effects of the one before. They rightly infer that some thorough reform is needed, one that will end speculation on public measures, inspire general prudence and industry, and give the business of society a regular course. The prohibition on titles of nobility is copied from the Articles of Confederation and needs no comment.

2. "No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce of all duties and imposts laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

Every argument that proves trade must be regulated in the federal councils also supports the restraint on the States' power over imports and exports. There is therefore no need to say more on this point, except that the way the restraint is qualified seems well designed to do two things at once. It secures to the States a reasonable discretion in providing for the convenience of their imports and exports, and it gives the United States a reasonable check against abuse of that discretion. The remaining particulars of this clause fall under reasonings that are either so obvious or so fully developed already that they may be passed over without remark.
The SIXTH and last class consists of the various powers and provisions that give effect to all the rest.

1. The first of these is the "power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof."

Few parts of the Constitution have been attacked more intemperately than this one, yet on fair investigation no part appears more completely invulnerable. Without the SUBSTANCE of this power, the whole Constitution would be a dead letter. Those who object to the article can therefore only mean that the FORM of the provision is wrong. But have they considered whether a better form could have been found?

The Constitution might have dealt with this subject in four other ways. It might have copied the second article of the existing Confederation, which would have forbidden the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated. It might have tried to list positively the powers comprehended in the general terms "necessary and proper." It might have tried to list them negatively, by naming the powers excepted from the general definition. Or it might have said nothing at all, leaving these necessary and proper powers to construction and inference.

Suppose the Convention had taken the first course and adopted the second article of the Confederation. It is evident that the new Congress, like its predecessors, would constantly face a choice between two alternatives. It could read the word "EXPRESSLY" so strictly that the government was left with no real authority at all, or so loosely that the restriction lost all its force. It would be easy to show, if it were necessary, that Congress has never been able, and never will be able, to carry out any important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation without turning, more or less, to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. The powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, so the government administering it would be still more hard pressed by the alternative of betraying the public interests by doing nothing, or violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are indispensably necessary and proper but not EXPRESSLY granted.

Suppose the Convention had tried to list positively the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect. The attempt would have required a complete digest of the laws on every subject the Constitution touches. And that digest would have had to fit not only the present state of things but every possible change the future may bring. For whenever a general power is newly applied, the PARTICULAR POWERS that serve as means to the OBJECT of the general power must always vary with that object. They must often properly be varied even while the object remains the same.

Suppose they had tried instead to list the particular powers or means that are not necessary or proper for carrying the general powers into execution. The task would have been no less chimerical, and open to a further objection: every gap in the list would have amounted to a positive grant of authority. To avoid this, they might have listed only some of the exceptions and described all the rest by the general words NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER. Then the list would have covered only a few of the excepted powers. These would be the ones least likely to be assumed or tolerated, because a list would naturally pick out those that are least necessary or proper. And the unnecessary and improper powers left in the unlisted remainder would be less firmly excepted than if no partial list had been made at all.

Had the Constitution said nothing on this head, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers needed as means of executing the general powers would have passed to the government by unavoidable implication. No axiom is more clearly established in law or in reason than this: wherever the end is required, the means are authorized, and wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary to do it is included. Had the Convention followed this last course, then, every objection now raised against their plan would remain as plausible as ever. And there would be a real drawback: a pretext would be left standing which can be seized on at critical moments to call into question the essential powers of the Union.

Someone may ask what will follow if Congress misconstrues this part of the Constitution and exercises powers its true meaning does not warrant. I answer that the result will be the same as if Congress misconstrued or enlarged any other power vested in it. It will be the same as if the general power had been broken down into particulars and one of those particulars were violated. In short, it will be the same as if the State legislatures should violate their own constitutional authorities. In the first case, whether the usurpation succeeds will depend on the executive and judiciary departments, which expound and give effect to the legislative acts. In the last resort, the remedy must come from the people, who can annul the acts of the usurpers by electing more faithful representatives. The truth is that we can rely on this ultimate redress more against unconstitutional acts of the federal legislature than against those of the State legislatures, for a plain reason. Every such federal act will invade the rights of the State legislatures, and they will always be ready to point out the innovation, to sound the alarm to the people, and to use their local influence to bring about a change of federal representatives. There is no such intermediate body, between the State legislatures and the people, with an interest in watching the conduct of the former. Violations of the State constitutions are therefore more likely to go unnoticed and unredressed.

2. "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

The indiscreet zeal of the Constitution's opponents has led them to attack this part of it as well, though without it the Constitution would plainly and radically be defective. To see this fully, we need only suppose for a moment that a clause saving the State constitutions had left their supremacy intact.

First, these constitutions give the State legislatures absolute sovereignty in all cases the existing Articles of Confederation do not except. Every authority in the proposed Constitution that goes beyond those listed in the Confederation would therefore have been nullified, and the new Congress would have been left as powerless as its predecessors.

Second, the constitutions of some of the States do not even expressly and fully recognize the existing powers of the Confederacy. In those States, an express saving of the supremacy of the State constitutions would have called into question every power in the proposed Constitution.

Third, the State constitutions differ greatly from one another. A treaty or national law of great and equal importance to all the States might therefore conflict with some constitutions and not with others. It would then be valid in some of the States and have no effect in others.

In short, the world would have seen, for the first time, a system of government founded on an inversion of the fundamental principles of all government. It would have seen the authority of the whole society everywhere subordinate to the authority of the parts. It would have seen a monster whose head took its orders from its limbs.

3. "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."

Some have asked why it was thought necessary to bind the State officials to support the federal Constitution, yet unnecessary to impose a like oath on the officers of the United States in favor of the State constitutions.

Several reasons might be given for the distinction. I will content myself with one, which is obvious and conclusive. The members of the federal government will have no part in putting the State constitutions into effect. The members and officers of the State governments, on the contrary, will play an essential part in putting the federal Constitution into effect. The election of the President and Senate will depend in every case on the legislatures of the individual States. The election of the House of Representatives will likewise depend on the same authority at first, and will probably always be conducted by State officers and under State laws.

4. Among the provisions for making the federal powers effective we might add those that belong to the executive and judiciary departments. But since these are reserved for particular examination elsewhere, I pass them over here.

We have now reviewed in detail all the articles that make up the sum of power the proposed Constitution delegates to the federal government. They bring us to this undeniable conclusion: no part of that power is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union. The question whether to grant this amount of power therefore comes down to another: whether to establish a government equal to the needs of the Union, or, in other words, whether the Union itself shall be preserved.
